prompt: What makes a molecule chiral?

choices.text: It is non-superimposable on its mirror image
It contains a metal atom
choices.why: Many chiral molecules have no metal, and many metal complexes aren't chiral. Chirality means being non-superimposable on the mirror image.

choices.text: It has a mirror plane
choices.why: The opposite: a chiral molecule cannot have a plane of symmetry.

choices.text: It has a center of inversion
choices.why: A molecule with an inversion center can't be chiral.

explanation: A molecule is chiral (or dissymmetric) if it is non-superimposable on its mirror image. The two mirror-image forms are called enantiomers.

prompt: How do two enantiomers differ?

choices.text: They rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions and react differently with other chiral molecules
They have different melting points
choices.why: Enantiomers have the same physical properties, such as melting point.

choices.text: They have different molecular formulas
choices.why: Enantiomers are mirror images, with the same atoms and connections.

choices.text: They don't differ in any way
choices.why: They differ in rotating plane-polarized light and in their reactivity with other chiral molecules.

explanation: Enantiomers have the same physical properties, such as melting point. They differ in their ability to rotate plane-polarized light, which makes them optically active, and in their reactivity with other chiral molecules.

prompt: What did Louis Pasteur observe around 1847 with the crystals of tartaric acid salts that he separated?

choices.text: The two types rotated plane-polarized light by the same amount but in opposite directions
The two types had different chemical formulas
choices.why: The two crystal types were enantiomers, mirror-image forms of the same compound.

choices.text: Only one type rotated plane-polarized light
choices.why: Both rotated it, by the same amount, in different directions.

choices.text: The two types had different melting points
choices.why: Enantiomers have the same physical properties. What Pasteur saw was opposite rotation of plane-polarized light.

explanation: Pasteur used tweezers to separate two types of crystals that precipitated, and found that they rotated plane-polarized light by the same amount but in different directions. These two compounds are enantiomers.

prompt: Which symmetry elements must a molecule lack to be chiral?

choices.text: Every improper axis S_n, including mirror planes (S1) and an inversion center (S2)
Proper rotation axes (C_n)
choices.why: Chiral molecules can have proper rotation axes: [Co(en)3]^3+ is chiral and has C3 and C2 axes.

choices.text: Only mirror planes
choices.why: A molecule with no mirror plane but an inversion center, or an S4 axis, is still achiral. A chiral molecule has no S_n of any order.

choices.text: The identity
choices.why: Every molecule has the identity.

explanation: A chiral molecule cannot have a plane of symmetry (σ), a center of inversion (i), or an improper axis (S_n). Since σ = S1 and i = S2, the rule is: a molecule is chiral if and only if its point group has no S_n axis of any order.

prompt: Which of these point groups could a chiral molecule have?

choices.text: D3
C2v
choices.why: C2v has mirror planes, so molecules in it are achiral.

choices.text: D3h
choices.why: D3h has a horizontal mirror plane, so its molecules are achiral.

choices.text: Cs
choices.why: Cs has a mirror plane, so its molecules are achiral.

explanation: Point groups with no improper axis are C1, C_n, D_n, T, O, and I. D3 is one: [Co(en)3]^3+, a D3 ion, exists as two chiral enantiomers, Δ and Λ.

prompt: The Δ and Λ isomers of [Co(en)3]^3+ can be pictured as fan blades. To push air toward you, which way would you turn the Δ isomer?

choices.text: Clockwise
Counterclockwise
choices.why: That's the Λ isomer. The Δ isomer would be turned clockwise to push air toward you.

choices.text: Either way
choices.why: The two isomers are mirror images, so they have opposite handedness: Δ clockwise, Λ counterclockwise.

explanation: Imagining the ligands as fan blades, you would rotate the Δ isomer clockwise and the Λ isomer counterclockwise to push the air toward you. The two are enantiomers.

prompt: How many vibrational modes does ammonia, NH3 (a nonlinear molecule with 4 atoms), have?
explanation: A nonlinear molecule has 3N − 6 vibrations: 3(4) − 6 = 12 − 6 = 6.

prompt: How many vibrational modes does carbon dioxide, CO2 (a linear molecule with 3 atoms), have?
explanation: A linear molecule has 3N − 5 vibrations: 3(3) − 5 = 9 − 5 = 4.

prompt: Why do linear molecules have 3N − 5 vibrations, while nonlinear molecules have 3N − 6?

choices.text: Linear molecules have two rotational degrees of freedom; nonlinear molecules have three
Linear molecules have one fewer translation
choices.why: Every molecule has three translations, in x, y, and z. The difference is in rotations: two for linear, three for nonlinear.

choices.text: Linear molecules have one more atom
choices.why: N already counts the atoms. The difference is that linear molecules have only two rotations.

choices.text: Linear molecules can't vibrate along their axis
choices.why: They can. The formula differs because linear molecules have two rotational degrees of freedom instead of three.

explanation: Each atom can move in x, y, and z, so there are 3N degrees of freedom: three translations, two or three rotations, and the rest vibrations. Linear molecules have two rotations (3N − 5 vibrations); nonlinear ones three (3N − 6).

prompt: When finding the characters of Γ_modes, what does an atom that is moved to a new position by an operation contribute?

choices.text: Zero
3, one for each of its axes
choices.why: An atom contributes only if it stays in place. If it moves, its entries lie off the diagonal of the matrix, so it contributes zero to the trace.
−1 is for an axis on an atom that stays put but is turned into its own negative. An atom that moves contributes zero.
1 is for an axis on an unmoved atom that stays unchanged. A moved atom contributes zero.

explanation: If an atom moves away from itself, its non-zero matrix entries are off the diagonal, so it contributes zero to the character. If it stays in place, each of its axes contributes cos θ: 1 for unchanged, −1 for reversed.

prompt: What is the character of Γ_modes for NH3 (4 atoms) under the identity operation, E?
explanation: Under E every atom stays in place and all three of its axes are unchanged, each contributing cos(0°) = 1. With 4 atoms × 3 axes, the character is 12, equal to 3N.

prompt: In C2v (h = 4, one operation per class), a reducible representation has characters 4, 0, 2, 2 under E, C2, σv, σv'. A1 has characters 1, 1, 1, 1. Using # of i = (1/h) Σ (operations in class) × χΓ × χi, how many times does A1 appear?
For water, Γ_modes = 3A1 + A2 + 3B1 + 2B2. After subtracting the translations (A1 + B1 + B2) and rotations (A2 + B1 + B2), what are the vibrations?

choices.why: That subtracts nothing from A1 and B1. Removing one A1 (translation) and two B1 (translation and rotation) leaves 2A1 + B1.
Water's single A2 is a rotation (Rz), so no A2 remains. The vibrations are 2A1 + B1.
Both B2s are used up, one as a translation (y) and one as a rotation (Rx). The vibrations are 2A1 + B1.

explanation: (3A1 + A2 + 3B1 + 2B2) − (A1 + B1 + B2) − (A2 + B1 + B2) = 2A1 + B1. That's three vibrations, matching 3N − 6 = 3 for water.

prompt: What makes a vibration IR-active, and how do you spot it in a character table?

choices.text: It changes the dipole moment; its irreducible representation has the symmetry of x, y, or z
It changes the polarizability; its representation matches a binary product
choices.why: That's the Raman selection rule. IR activity needs a change in dipole moment, shown by x, y, or z.

choices.text: It is totally symmetric
choices.why: IR activity depends on the representation matching x, y, or z. In C2v, B1 and B2 vibrations are IR-active too.

choices.text: Every vibration is IR-active
choices.why: Only vibrations that change the dipole moment are, as with the B3u but not the Ag CO stretch of trans-ML2(CO)2.

explanation: A vibration that changes the molecular dipole moment is IR-active; in the character table these are the representations with the symmetry of x, y, or z. A vibration that changes the polarizability is Raman-active, shown by the binary products.

prompt: Water's vibrations are 2A1 + B1. In C2v, A1 and B1 are both IR- and Raman-active. How many IR and Raman peaks are possible?

choices.text: Three IR peaks and three Raman peaks
Two IR peaks and one Raman peak
choices.why: All three vibrations (two A1 and one B1) are both IR- and Raman-active.

choices.text: One IR peak and one Raman peak
choices.why: Each of the three vibrations can give a peak in both spectra.

choices.text: No IR peaks, because water is symmetric
choices.why: A1 has z symmetry and B1 has x symmetry, so all three vibrations are IR-active.

explanation: Both A1 and B1 are IR-active (they match z and x) and Raman-active (they match binary products), so three IR peaks and three Raman peaks are possible for water.

prompt: Group theory predicts three possible IR peaks for a molecule, but the measured spectrum shows only two. What is a likely explanation?

choices.text: Two peaks overlap, or one is off-scale: group theory gives what is possible, not what is seen
The group theory analysis must be wrong
choices.why: Not necessarily. The prediction gives possible peaks; overlapping or off-scale peaks can hide one.

choices.text: The molecule must have lost an atom
choices.why: Overlapping or off-scale peaks are a much simpler explanation. Group theory predicts what's possible, not what's observed.

explanation: Group theory tells what is possible, not what will actually appear. If two IR peaks overlap, only one might be noticed; a peak that is off-scale wouldn't be seen in the data.

prompt: Which of water's vibrations has B1 symmetry?

choices.text: The antisymmetric stretch
The symmetric stretch
choices.why: The symmetric stretch is completely symmetric, A1.

choices.text: The symmetric bend
choices.why: The symmetric bend is completely symmetric, A1.

choices.text: None: B1 is a rotation
choices.why: One of water's B1 representations is a rotation (Ry) and one a translation (x), but one B1 remains as a vibration: the antisymmetric stretch.

explanation: The two A1 vibrations are completely symmetric: a symmetric stretch and a symmetric bend. The B1 vibration, antisymmetric with respect to the C2 axis, is the antisymmetric stretch.

prompt: What are the point groups of the cis and trans isomers of square planar ML2(CO)2?

choices.text: cis is C2v; trans is D2h
cis is D2h; trans is C2v
choices.why: This is reversed. The trans isomer, with identical groups opposite each other, has the higher D2h symmetry.

choices.text: Both are D4h
choices.why: D4h needs four identical ligands, like [PtCl4]^2−. With two L and two CO, the isomers are C2v (cis) and D2h (trans).

choices.text: Both are C2v
choices.why: The trans isomer has an inversion center and perpendicular C2 axes: D2h.

explanation: The cis isomer of square planar ML2(CO)2 has C2v symmetry and the trans isomer has D2h symmetry.

prompt: The CO stretches of cis-ML2(CO)2 have A1 and B1 symmetry, both IR-active in C2v. How many CO stretching bands are possible in its IR spectrum?
explanation: A1 and B1 are both IR-active (and Raman-active) in C2v, and each is singly degenerate, so two CO bands are possible in the IR spectrum, and two in the Raman.

prompt: The CO stretches of trans-ML2(CO)2 have Ag and B3u symmetry. What can each spectrum show?

choices.text: One IR band (B3u) and one Raman band (Ag)
Two IR bands and two Raman bands
choices.why: That's the cis isomer. In trans, Ag is Raman-active only and B3u IR-active only.

choices.text: Two IR bands and no Raman bands
choices.why: Ag has the symmetry of binary products, so it is Raman-active: one band in each spectrum.

choices.text: No bands in either spectrum
choices.why: B3u has x symmetry (IR-active) and Ag has x^2, y^2, z^2 symmetry (Raman-active): one band each.

explanation: Under D2h, the Ag CO stretch is Raman-active only and the B3u stretch is IR-active only. So only one IR band and one Raman band are possible for the trans isomer.

prompt: A pure sample of ML2(CO)2 shows two CO stretching bands in its IR spectrum. What can you conclude?

choices.text: It isn't the trans isomer, which can give only one IR CO band
It must be the trans isomer
choices.why: The trans isomer can show only one IR CO band (B3u). Two bands rule it out.

choices.text: Nothing: both isomers give two bands
choices.why: The cis isomer can give two IR CO bands, the trans only one, so the count distinguishes them.

explanation: The cis isomer can produce two CO stretches in an IR (or Raman) spectrum, while the trans isomer can produce only one. Two CO stretching bands rule out a pure sample of trans-ML2(CO)2.

prompt: The CO stretches of fac-ML3(CO)3 are A1 + E, and those of mer-ML3(CO)3 are 2A1 + B1, all IR-active. A degenerate E pair gives a single band. How do their IR spectra compare?

choices.text: fac can show two CO bands and mer three, so IR can tell them apart
Both can show three CO bands, so IR can't tell them apart
choices.why: That's what the section's answer says, but its note corrects it: E is one band, so fac gives two bands and mer three.

choices.text: fac can show three CO bands and mer two
choices.why: fac's A1 + E gives two bands (the E pair is one band); mer's 2A1 + B1 gives three.

choices.text: Neither shows any CO bands
choices.why: A1, E, and B1 are all IR-active here, so both isomers show CO bands: two for fac, three for mer.

explanation: fac-ML3(CO)3 (C3v) has A1 + E CO stretches: two IR bands, since the degenerate E pair gives one band. mer-ML3(CO)3 (C2v) has 2A1 + B1: three bands. As the section's note explains, the band count does distinguish the isomers.

prompt: When analyzing only the CO stretches of a metal carbonyl, why don't you subtract rotations and translations?

choices.text: The CO stretching vectors describe only motions of the C–O groups, not of the whole molecule
Metal carbonyls don't rotate or translate
choices.why: They do. But a Γ built from C–O bond vectors includes only C–O stretches, so there is nothing to subtract.

choices.text: Rotations and translations are always IR-inactive
choices.why: The reason is that a Γ from C–O bond vectors contains only stretching motions of those bonds.

explanation: In this method, a vector along each C–O bond gets 1 if it stays in place under an operation and 0 if it moves. The resulting representation covers only the C–O stretches, isolated to the CO groups, so it contains no rotations or translations to subtract.

prompt: What is the point group of the square planar ion tetrachloroplatinate(II), [PtCl4]^2−?

choices.text: D4h
Td
choices.why: Td is for tetrahedral molecules like CH4. [PtCl4]^2− is square planar.

choices.text: C4v
choices.why: [PtCl4]^2− also has perpendicular C2 axes and a horizontal mirror plane (the molecular plane): D4h.

choices.text: D2h
choices.why: D2h fits trans-ML2(CO)2. With four identical ligands, [PtCl4]^2− has a C4 axis: D4h.

explanation: Square planar [PtCl4]^2− is in the D4h point group. With 5 atoms it has 15 degrees of freedom, and its Γ_modes is built with the D4h character table.
